idiom_name: single-owner worker/task with message passing (no shared lock)
implementation_notes: JavaScript's ordinary execution model is one thread with an event loop: there is no synchronously acquirable lock over shared mutable state, so the problem the pattern solves - a component re-acquiring a lock it already holds - does not arise in normal code, and the interleaving that does happen occurs at await and microtask boundaries, which a lock discipline does not address. Where several agents genuinely share memory (workers plus SharedArrayBuffer) the platform supplies Atomics, i.e. lock-free primitives, and Atomics.wait is unavailable on the main thread; async mutex libraries reintroduce exactly the non-reentrant-lock deadlock the pattern describes, with no language support for the split. The honest adaptation is ownership transfer: one owner per component, messages in, results out.
pitfalls: An async mutex (the recurring 'one lock per component' workaround) is not reentrant: a public async method that awaits another public method of the same component waits on a lock its own caller holds and never resolves.
A lock released between awaits does not protect the invariant across the await - the state can interleave even while the critical section appears to be running.
SharedArrayBuffer requires cross-origin isolation and Atomics.wait throws on the main thread; Atomics.waitAsync changes the shape of the code entirely.
structuredClone (postMessage) cannot carry functions, class instances or Maps of class instances, so the state must be plain data before ownership moves.
alternative: Do not share the component's mutable state between agents: keep the state in one worker (or one async task) and let callers send messages - postMessage/structuredClone between workers, or a serialized promise queue inside one thread - so there is no lock to re-acquire. If a shared-memory buffer is unavoidable, use Atomics (compareExchange/wait/notify) for lock-free hand-off rather than a hand-written re-entrant lock.
